chapter.name: Concept of the Constitution
chapter.blurb: The meaning, functions, qualities and classification of constitutions, and constitutionalism.

concepts.name: Meaning and definitions of a constitution
concepts.description: The origin of the word, the many names for a constitution and the views of Gilchrist, Gettell, Wheare and Wade and Phillips.
concepts.idea: A constitution is the set of fundamental rules on how government is organised and how it relates to the people.
concepts.rule: The word constitution comes from the Latin constituere, meaning to establish or set up. A constitution is a set of principles that specify how government is organised and works and the relationship between government and people in terms of rights and duties. It is called the fundamental law of the land, supreme law of the state, basic law, instrument of government, rules of the state, basic structure of the polity and grundnorm. Gilchrist sees it as the rules that fix the organisation of government, the distribution of powers and the general principles for using them. Gettell stresses the fundamental principles that determine the form of a state. Wheare describes the whole system of government, the rules that establish and regulate the government. Wade and Phillips call it a document with special legal sanctity that sets out the framework and main functions of the organs of government and the principles of their operation.
concepts.example: Wheare describes a constitution as the collection of rules which establish and regulate the government.

concepts.name: Functions of a constitution
concepts.description: The purposes of a constitution as identified by Elliot Bulmer.
concepts.idea: A constitution defines the political community, rights and institutions, and can set social and economic goals.
concepts.rule: Elliot Bulmer lists functions of a constitution: it can declare and define the boundaries of the political community and its nature and authority; express the identity and values of a national community; declare and define the rights and duties of citizens; establish and regulate political institutions; divide or share power between different layers of government or sub-state communities; declare the official religious identity of the state and the relationship between sacred and secular authority; and commit the state to particular social, economic or developmental goals.
concepts.example: A constitution that promises social and economic development commits the state to particular goals.

concepts.name: Qualities of a good constitution
concepts.description: Brevity, clarity, definiteness, comprehensiveness, suitability, stability and adaptability.
concepts.idea: A good constitution is clear, complete and suitable, yet stable and able to adapt.
concepts.rule: The qualities of a good constitution are: brevity, meaning it is precise and does not carry unwanted detail; clarity, using plain terms; definiteness, giving provisions a definite meaning so judges have less discretion; comprehensiveness, covering powers of government and rights and duties of citizens to reduce disputes; suitability, reflecting the needs, history and conditions of the people; stability, so it is not easily tampered with; and adaptability, so it is dynamic and a living document that can change with new needs.
concepts.example: A lengthy constitution with many details may create confusion in interpreting its clauses.

concepts.name: Classification: evolved or enacted, written or unwritten
concepts.description: Types of constitution by evolution and by incorporation of provisions, with examples.
concepts.idea: Constitutions are evolved or enacted, and written or unwritten, with the British and Indian ones as key examples.
concepts.rule: On the basis of evolution, an evolved constitution grows slowly through conventions, practices, principles and judicial decisions; it is also called cumulative, and the British Constitution is an example. An enacted constitution is deliberately made by a constituent assembly or council, or promulgated by a king or Parliament, and its provisions are in a book or documents; it is also called conventional, and the American and Indian Constitutions are examples. On the basis of incorporation, a written constitution is put together in a document or series of documents, formulated by a constituent assembly or convention, and is also called documentary or codified, as in the USA, Canada, Japan, France and India. An unwritten constitution consists mostly of conventions, practices, principles, charters, statutes and judicial decisions, is non-documentary or uncodified, and is found in the UK, New Zealand and Israel. The written-unwritten distinction is broadly similar to the enacted-evolved one.
concepts.example: The British Constitution is a standard example of an evolved, unwritten constitution.

concepts.name: Classification: rigid or flexible, federal or unitary, procedural or prescriptive
concepts.description: Types by method of amendment, by division of power and by nature and purpose.
concepts.idea: Constitutions differ in how they are amended, how power is divided and what they aim to do.
concepts.rule: Lord James Bryce classified constitutions by method of amendment. A rigid constitution cannot be amended like ordinary laws and needs a special procedure, so it separates constitutional law from ordinary law (USA, Australia, Switzerland). A flexible constitution can be amended like ordinary laws (UK, New Zealand). India's Constitution is neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis of both. Federal constitutions divide power between the national and regional governments who operate independently in their fields (USA, Switzerland, Australia, Canada, Russia, Brazil), while unitary constitutions concentrate power in the national government and regional governments act as subordinate agencies (UK, France, Japan, China, Italy, Norway). India has both federal and unitary features and K.C. Wheare called it quasi-federal. Elliot Bulmer identified procedural and prescriptive constitutions: a procedural constitution defines the structure of institutions and legal limits of government power to protect democratic processes and human rights, while a prescriptive one also assumes or imposes a broad consensus on common societal goals that authorities must pursue.
concepts.example: K.C. Wheare called the Indian Constitution quasi-federal.

concepts.name: Constitutionalism and constitutional government
concepts.description: Limited government, the definitions of Friedrich, Roucek, Wheare and Ybema, and Louis Henkin's eight elements.
concepts.idea: Constitutionalism means limited government under rules, not just having a constitution.
concepts.rule: A country may have a constitution without constitutionalism, as in a dictatorship. Constitutionalism means limited government, the opposite of arbitrary power, and holds that those who govern must follow laws and rules. Constitutional government must be democratic, and arbitrary power even if conferred by a constitutional document negates constitutionalism. Friedrich sees constitutionalism as a system of effective restraints on governmental action. Roucek calls it essentially limited government, the antithesis of government by the unrestrained will of rulers. Wheare says constitutional government is government according to rule and limited by the constitution, not just by the desires and capacities of those who exercise power. Ybema says government is constitutional only when rulers are subject to rules and principles that limit their power. Louis Henkin identified eight elements: popular sovereignty, rule of law, democratic (responsible and accountable) government, separation of powers with checks and balances, an independent judiciary, civilian control of the military, police governed by law and judicial control, and respect for individual rights.
concepts.example: A dictatorship may have a constitution but not constitutionalism.
